name: Karl Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we run no sales or campaigns. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a brass section for concerts, play trumpet on commercial recordings and teach four advanced pupils. Morning is a score and a school run, afternoon is a rehearsal, and some nights end with a studio call. I love finding a phrase that makes three horns sound like one, but the last-minute recording changes wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do work and home money fit together?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a paramedic, and our two children still need pickup between shifts. We have a mortgage and about eight months of expenses saved; the concert and recording rates are good, and nearby venues do hire. I have a music master’s, use AI every day for timetables and rough score checks, but my trumpet and the final ear are mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a quicker invoice is useful and a live horn line still needs a player. I already use AI to sort calls and check a rough score, then read every part myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The concert dates and four pupils look steady, and my partner’s pay is regular. The mortgage is real, but eight months in reserve and higher fees leave me comfortable with ordinary ups and downs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep my booked concerts, recording calls and four pupils, checking each invoice against the agreed playing and preparation fee. Through the first year of a plateau I would keep that work and save one fifth of each cleared extra studio fee after mortgage, food and childcare toward a twelve-month reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our work and income here. I would rather count cleared fees than boast about a calendar full of pencilled dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets checked on an invoice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The session, setup and any extra arrangement time each need a line. A booking is not income until the fee is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another microphone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if paid sessions actually need it and the price leaves the mortgage and reserve untouched. At present my existing kit earns its keep.

I would count **paid sessions**, not tentative dates.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** and current fees cover normal changes.
I still have to watch **mortgage costs** and unpaid preparation.
do: Keep **concerts and pupils** with recording calls and checked playing and preparation fees.
Save **one fifth** of cleared extra studio fees after essentials toward twelve months of expenses.
feel: I feel **calm** about current work and household income.

fieldNote: His **daily AI use** already helps with scheduling and rough scores, followed by his own checking.
The **eight-month reserve** and paid dates make a plateau comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say software can write a brass sketch faster than my old pencil, but clients must know who owns the sound. I would show colleagues a new mixing method only on recordings the players let me use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Commercial buyers may stop paying for short horn lines, and that is part of my income. Live shows and lessons should last longer, though I cannot pay the mortgage with applause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I would learn to separate and clean tracks with AI on my own licensed trumpet recordings, with the engineer’s help, and check every note by ear before delivery. If two quarters of paid jingle calls fall, I would offer a separate horn-recording service only after six signed client commissions and deposits cover my playing and preparation, an engineer’s paid time, gear rental and confirmed childcare; I would repeat in the first year only on those terms, keeping paid concerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about jingle fees shrinking. We have eight months saved. A tool is only useful if six real customers pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose files go into the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only mine or tracks whose players and clients give written permission. I would keep private sessions off any public upload service and compare the output to the original recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a booth now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Six signed commissions would pay for rented gear first; I would not take a booth lease against imagined demand.

feel: I feel **anxious** about a plausible loss of commercial fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that 2028 thinking AGI could price and build recordings before a robot can hold a horn around 2031. We need signed playing rates, not guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think paid commercial calls could fall quickly in 2028. The main concert chair gives us time, but losing that recording line would cut real household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get the concert and pupil dates in writing and keep delivering paid recordings. In the first year after 2028, if jingle orders stop and live dates also shrink, I would apply for a posted paid band-director role only if my master’s meets its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and pickup is covered; I would keep concerts and pupils until a signed offer is in hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the speed of lost work, though local halls and schools give me options. Plenty of jobs nearby is not the same as a posted job at the right rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the first school offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would count paid hours, preparation and travel against what I lose before signing. My partner’s ambulance shift cannot be my unplanned childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do robots enter this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Around 2031 for capable stage playing, if the card holds. The commercial recording and booking decisions could change in 2028, so my first pay check is there.

I would press for **signed playing rates** at the hall.
think: I expect **commercial calls** to fall and live dates could shrink.
A nearby **director job** matters only if posted and paid adequately.
do: Keep **concerts and pupils** until a signed replacement offer; confirm dates before 2028.
Seek **posted band-director role** after jingle/live losses only with qualifying master’s, written replacement net after travel and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a fast cut to household fees.
S2.quote: Plenty of jobs nearby is not the same as a posted job at the right rate.
fieldNote: His **2028 risk** is commercial recording income, before robot horn playing around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets musicians agree what their recordings may be used for. A new tool should carry names and fees, not erase them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect commercial horn sessions to lose orders by 2031, but live stages may carry on before robot players around 2034. That gives me time to see if buyers will pay for recordings with actual players.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would study track cleaning on my own licensed files and ask the engineer to teach me where it fails, checking every delivered note myself. If two quarters of jingle income drop, I would launch a separate player-led recording service only after six signed paid commissions cover my playing and preparation, the engineer, rented kit and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2031 I would continue only if six jobs meet that floor and keep concerts that pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a large part of a studio week might disappear. I can test demand over five years. I cannot declare a real market into existence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if clients ask for an imitation of another player?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would turn it down without the player’s written consent and a fee for the use. My own files are enough to test a mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only two commissions arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish those on existing terms and skip the separate service and gear rental. Two jobs cannot cover the engineer and my preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children that the 2036 thinking change and robot players around 2039 are separate dates. I would also tell them to ask who is paid when a recording is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still lead horns on stage, but commercial sessions could pay much less. My partner’s wage and eight months saved keep the next few years steady, not every year to come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid concerts and four pupils and save a fifth of cleared extra service profit after engineer, rentals, my playing and preparation, childcare, mortgage and food toward twelve months. Over the decade I would run the separate service only with six signed commissions, licensed player files, written use permission and fees covering all those costs; in the first year after 2036 I would continue only while that floor holds and seek a posted paid director job if jingle and live fees fall, with an accepted master’s, written net pay after travel replacing losses and pickup covered, keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of studio work. Our present income is solid, but I want contracts and paid players before I put family money into gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a recording room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a run of actual paid work covered a lease without touching our eight-month reserve. For now rented kit and the engineer’s room are enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train your children on the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they want to learn music, I would first teach them to hear a line and know whose recording it is. Software can come after that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because commercial fees could vanish before I have six replacement clients. Signed concert work, a real posted director vacancy if needed, and written permission and fees for each player would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the recording before asking what a machine can do with it. A musician can be paid for a note once and then lose every later use if the terms are vague.

headlineQuote: A musician can be paid for a note once and then lose every later use if the terms are vague.
portrait: Karl is a **senior trumpet leader** with a master’s, four pupils and well-paid concert and studio work.
His **eight-month reserve**, paramedic partner, two schoolchildren and mortgage shape his room for risk.
He learns **licensed track cleaning** beyond his daily scheduling and score checks, with manual listening.
He tests **player-led recordings** only when six paid commissions cover both musicians and family costs.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove commercial fees before six replacement clients exist.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **signed concert work**, a real director vacancy if needed and written player-use fees.
